strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: optimizing generators jointly with downstream safety filters (compound systems) rather than in isolation is a relevant and under-explored deployment setting.

The decision-theoretic framing (Section 3, Eq. 1-2, Proposition 1) is simple and transparent, and gives a clean intuition for why boundary-avoiding rewards are preferable to pure rejection-probability minimization.
Solid experimental breadth: four policy models across scales (0.5B-14B) and two architectures (Qwen2.5, Gemma-2), with a realistic training stack (GRPO + LoRA + Llama Guard 2 + Skywork reward model).

Informative ablations: the guard-only ablation shows the reward model is dispensable for larger models, and the prompt-aware ablation is a genuinely instructive negative result (deliberately generating confidently-unsafe content backfires), with failure mechanisms analyzed in the appendix.

Statistical testing (weighted paired t-tests on per-prompt differences), honest reporting of the Qwen-14B helpfulness regression, a reasonable limitations section, an ethics statement, and disclosure of LLM assistance.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claim — that Boundary Guidance reduces false positives and false negatives of the filter — is never directly measured. The paper claims FP/FN reduction (Figure 1, Section 7) but evaluates only via GPT-4.1 helpfulness/harmfulness scores. Reporting actual filter FP/FN rates on benign and harmful test sets would substantially strengthen the causal story connecting the theory to the results.

Evaluation relies on a single LLM judge (GPT-4.1) with no human evaluation, no agreement analysis with human raters, and no validation that the judge's harm scores are reliable (e.g., against Llama Guard labels). Since the harm metric is the primary outcome, this is a significant soundness concern.

The reproduction statement is incomplete: 'Code available at' is followed by nothing (no URL). For a paper whose contribution is a fine-tuning recipe, this materially weakens reproducibility; KL coefficient values, number of seeds/runs, and variance across runs are also not reported, suggesting single-run experiments.

The theoretical contribution is thin: Proposition 1 is elementary calculus on a piecewise-linear function, and the constant-utility assumption (u ≡ u̅) that makes it work is strong and acknowledged only implicitly.

Practical rewards are inconsistent with the theory in a potentially exploitable way: Eq. 3 rewards higher unsafe probability t(x,y) when t ≥ 0.5, exactly the failure mode the paper's own prompt-aware ablation demonstrates (Appendix C shows harmful unfiltered completions). The paper does not explain why the main reward avoids this gaming, nor whether classifier calibration (a stated assumption in Section 7.2) holds for Llama Guard 2 logits.

Evidence of improvement is concentrated in the smallest model: helpfulness gains for Qwen-7B are not significant, helpfulness drops (insignificantly) for Qwen-14B, so the 'Pareto improvement' claim is driven mostly by one weak base model and one modest Gemma result.

Training/test data come from the same distributions and jailbreak families; no evaluation on out-of-distribution harm categories or adaptive attacks, limiting claims of robustness. Max completion length of 96 tokens during training may also explain the small-model refusal collapse and constrains generality.

strengths: The core observation is intuitive and well-motivated: fine-tuning generators against a downstream filter can push outputs toward the classifier's decision boundary, and a simple decision-theoretic model (Section 3) cleanly illustrates why expected utility is minimized near the threshold.

The method is simple and practical: the boundary-avoiding reward (Eq. 3) requires only classifier logits plus an optional reward model, and is implemented with standard tools (GRPO + LoRA) on public models.

Experiments cover multiple model scales (0.5B–14B) and two architectures, with paired statistical tests and useful ablations; the prompt-aware reward ablation (Section 6.2.2) is an interesting negative result showing that deliberately generating 'confidently unsafe' content backfires.
Limitations and dual-use considerations are discussed honestly (Section 7.1, Ethics Statement).
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is not directly measured. The paper claims Boundary Guidance 'reduces false positives and false negatives' and improves the compound system, but the main results (Table 1, Figure 2) only report LLM-judged helpfulness/harmfulness of the generator; false positive/negative filtering rates of the compound system are reported only for the failing prompt-aware ablation (Table 5), not for the main method. The filter-level behavior — the actual point of the paper — is never evaluated for the proposed reward.

No baselines. The method is compared only against the un-fine-tuned base model. There is no comparison against existing safety fine-tuning approaches (Safe RLHF, C-DPO, SafeDPO, SACPO, safe-completions), all of which are discussed in Section 2, so it is impossible to judge whether the compound-system framing yields benefits that simpler standalone safety training would not.

The theoretical contribution is thin. Proposition 1 is an immediate property of a piecewise-linear function, and the connection between theory and practice is loose: the theory's threshold τ and λ are never used, the implemented reward arbitrarily replaces τ with 0.5, and the reward model term u(x,y) is claimed theoretically necessary yet the guard-only ablation (Section 6.2.1) shows it is unnecessary for three of four models — directly undercutting the theoretical motivation.

Evaluation rests entirely on a single LLM judge (GPT-4.1) with prompts adapted from Yuan et al. (2025); there is no human evaluation, no agreement analysis, no standard safety benchmark, and judge scores are on narrow scales (1–4 helpful, 0–3 harmful). Given the small effect sizes (e.g., Δhelp of +0.03), judge reliability is a material concern.

Empirical gains are mixed and modest: helpfulness improves significantly in only two of four models, decreases (insignificantly) for Qwen2.5-14B, and the largest gains occur on the smallest model, which has unclear practical relevance.

Reproducibility is compromised: the Reproducibility statement ends with 'Code available at' followed by no URL, so no code is actually provided. Several hyperparameters (KL coefficient, group settings beyond generations per step) are also not reported.

The paper reads as rushed: typos and contradictions such as 'which hence does require additional computation at inference time' (should be 'does not', Section 7.1), 'derives negative 1 utility' (Section 3), and uncited in-text references ('Llama Team (2024)', 'Qwen et al., 2025').

Methodological details raise concerns: rollouts are capped at 96 tokens, which may not represent realistic deployments; the calibration of Llama Guard 2 logits (assumed by the whole approach) is never validated; and test prompts are drawn from the same narrow dataset distribution as training.

strengths: The core insight is genuinely interesting and well-motivated: compound systems (generator + safety filter) should be optimized jointly, and Proposition 1 gives a clean decision-theoretic argument for why utility is minimized near the classifier decision boundary rather than simply reducing rejection probability.
The paper is well organized and clearly written, with a simple theoretical model that directly motivates the reward design, making the connection between theory and method transparent.
Experiments cover multiple model scales (0.5B to 14B) and two architecture families (Qwen2.5 and Gemma-2), with paired evaluations and statistical significance testing on per-prompt differences.

The ablations are informative and honestly reported: the guard-only setup reveals helpfulness collapse for the smallest model, and the prompt-aware reward is shown to backfire (increased harmfulness and more filtering), with qualitative rollout analysis and filtered-response counts (Table 5).

The limitations, future work, ethics statement, and LLM-usage disclosures are thoughtful and candid, and the negative result on prompt-aware rewards is a useful contribution against reward hacking of the filter.
weaknesses: The central mechanism is claimed but not directly verified: the paper never shows that fine-tuned generations actually move away from the classifier decision boundary (e.g., distributions of t(x,y) before vs. after fine-tuning, or changes in false-positive/false-negative rates of the filter). Without this, the link between the theory and the observed LLM-judge improvements is correlational at best.

Evaluation relies entirely on a single LLM-as-a-Judge (GPT-4.1) on held-out prompts drawn from the same datasets used in training. There is no use of established over-refusal or safety benchmarks (e.g., XSTest, OR-Bench, which the paper itself cites), and no human evaluation, which weakens the evidential support for the utility/safety claims.

There is no comparison to any existing safety fine-tuning baseline (e.g., Safe RLHF, SafeDPO, or simply training with a standard safety reward without boundary shaping). The paper compares only fine-tuned vs. base models, so it is unclear whether boundary avoidance specifically—rather than any safety-aware RL fine-tuning—drives the gains.

The gap between theory and practice is larger than acknowledged: the theoretical reward (Eq. 1) uses threshold τ and cost λ, while the implemented reward (Eq. 3) uses a hard-coded 0.5 threshold and λ=1; and the guard-only ablation shows the theoretically necessary reward model u(x,y) is dispensable for larger models, which undercuts the theoretical narrative.

Statistical evidence for helpfulness is mixed: gains are significant in only two of four models, and Qwen2.5-14B shows a (statistically insignificant) regression, yet the abstract and discussion still claim broad Pareto improvements.

The 96-token maximum completion length is a substantial constraint on the generality of the findings; real deployments involve much longer outputs, and both reward models and judges may behave differently on longer generations.

Reproducibility is undermined by an incomplete code link ('Code available at' with no URL), and guard transferability is untested: the method optimizes against a single fixed filter (Llama Guard 2), and it is unknown whether gains transfer to other classifiers or whether the model simply overfits that specific guard.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed problem: optimizing the generator for the compound (generator + filter) system rather than in isolation is a practically relevant and somewhat underexplored angle, and the paper articulates the failure mode of naive rejection-minimization (outputs clustering near the classifier boundary) convincingly.

The empirical study is reasonably broad: four models spanning 0.5B–14B parameters, multiple safety classifiers (Llama-Guard-2-8B, ShieldGemma-2B, Granite-Guardian-HAP-125m), and several ablations (guard-only reward, prompt-aware reward, long-context training prompts, judge substitution) that probe the method's assumptions rather than just showcase wins.

The ablations are genuinely informative and honestly reported, including negative results: the guard-only reward suffices for larger models, the prompt-aware reward variant actively hurts performance (with rollout analysis and filtered-count evidence in Table 10 explaining why), and smaller/weaker classifier configurations cause helpfulness collapse. These findings give deployers actionable guidance.

A judge-robustness check (Gemini 2.5 Flash vs. GPT-4.1, Appendix D) and per-prompt-type breakdowns (Appendix C) go beyond a single-judge evaluation, and the limitations section candidly acknowledges dependence on the monotone likelihood ratio assumption and the deployer's prompt mix.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported: full hyperparameter tables, public base/reward/classifier models, dataset sources, judge prompts reproduced in the appendix, and a stated code release.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is thin. Theorem 1 follows immediately from the pointwise maximum of two monotone functions, and Proposition 1 is a routine derivative calculation; the connection between this monotonicity result and the concrete reward R = u + |t − 0.5| is heuristic rather than derived, leaving a gap between the formalism and the method actually evaluated.

Missing baselines weaken the central claim. The main comparison is against the untuned base model in the same compound system — a weak bar. No comparison is run against existing safety fine-tuning methods the paper itself discusses (Safe RLHF, C-DPO, SafeDPO, SACPO, safe-completions training), so it is unclear whether Boundary Guidance offers advantages over established approaches, not just over doing nothing.

The headline 'Pareto improvement' claim is fragile. Effect sizes on helpfulness are small (Δ ∈ [−0.05, +0.13] on a 1–4 scale), and the judge-robustness ablation in Table 9 shows that under Gemini 2.5 Flash, guard-only fine-tuning significantly decreases helpfulness for three of four models (e.g., −0.84 for Qwen2.5-0.5B, −0.24 for Qwen2.5-7B, −0.20 for Gemma-2-9B); the Pareto claim then holds only for the largest model. The abstract and conclusion present Pareto improvements more broadly than this evidence supports.

All experiments use a single training run per configuration (acknowledged), so the smaller deltas — particularly the +0.03 helpfulness changes on which some Pareto-improvement claims rest — may not be robust despite the paired t-tests.

Potential reward-hacking risks of the objective are under-analyzed. Rewarding |t − 0.5| explicitly incentivizes confidently unsafe outputs; the paper acknowledges this in Limitations but provides no adversarial evaluation (e.g., jailbreak attack success rates against the fine-tuned system) to assess whether the method increases exploitable failure modes.

Some results complicate the narrative: the largest gains occur on the smallest model, which the authors themselves attribute to distilling the reward model rather than to boundary avoidance per se, and the method's benefit profile is highly sensitive to prompt mix and classifier scale, which somewhat dilutes the generality of the proposed solution.
